extracted.intended_audience: readers of political/literary essays and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A translated literary-political essay excerpt discussing the nature of war, the character of soldiers and generals, the role and membership of academies, and broader reflections on justice and society. Intended as a philosophical narrative rather than a formal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great_general_qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: A truly great commander must know not only the external shape of the land but also the customs and pursuits of peoples; he must retain innumerable small particulars from which he fashions broad views. His premeditated plans can be changed in the heat of battle by sudden inspiration; he is at once cautious and daring, sometimes slow as a snail, sometimes swift as a striking eagle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains concrete attributes distinguishing a superior military leader: deep geographic and ethnographic knowledge, memory for detail, capacity to form and adapt plans, and a mix of prudence and audacity. Use these dimensions to evaluate military leadership performance or historical generals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military_profession_critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Soldiering is presented as a degrading, often unthinking profession: the speaker finds military life repugnant because of its enslaving character, false honour, and associated cruelty. Soldiers tend to live in crowds, display ostentation (uniforms, ribbons), and their social position and honours often depend on vanity and superficial signs rather than intellect or virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a normative critique to judge the moral worth or social value of military institutions and of celebrating military status; useful for assessing cultural attitudes toward armed forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: War_justifications_and_abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Early wars arose from immediate necessities (settlement, food), but modern wars are often abuses: fought for colonies, trade, or pure plunder; princes steal provinces they do not need and destroy them for monuments. Thus many contemporary wars are base, pursued for vanity, profit, or spectacle rather than genuine necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A framework to distinguish 'legitimate' from 'abusive' wars in moral or historical analysis: examine motives (survival/settlement vs. commerce/vanity) and consequences (public benefit vs. gratuitous destruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic_value_of_war_vs_peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, war has been a school that produced civic virtues—patience, firmness, contempt of danger, self-sacrifice—and founded cities, laws and arts; yet in the author's time war has become a hereditary disease and a return to a savage life, a spectacle and pastime for courts rather than a public necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dual-evaluation criterion: acknowledge both war's formative civic roles in origin myths of states and its degeneration into anachronistic, harmful institutions in modernity. Use to weigh historical functions against present harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldier_vs_worker_nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: If nobility derived from exposure to danger were true, then peasants and laborers—who face daily risks from hunger and toil—would be nobler than soldiers; the supposed nobility of soldiers is mostly vanity because their dangers are episodic and limited compared with workers' continual peril.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a comparative moral yardstick for valuing professions: measure constancy and lived risk rather than theatrical or episodic bravery when assessing 'nobility' of occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human_law_vs_divine_law_on_right_and_wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker distinguishes human law from divine law, arguing that human notions of right and wrong are relative and debated chiefly by eloquence; people argue about justice with rhetoric, and one cannot definitively say laws are right or wrong apart from theological absolutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A principle for evaluating legal and moral claims: treat human law as contingent and rhetorical; be cautious in claiming absolute justice for positive laws without theological grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academy_mission_and_practical_role
rubrics_metrics.description: The academy's practical task is to collect and codify the living usages of language (compile the great dictionary) and to clean speech of old and vulgar impurities; it follows practice more than governs it. It is a society that also values fine manners and sociability among its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as criteria to evaluate literary or linguistic institutions: prioritize descriptive codification of current usage, social cohesion, and the cultivation of courteous behaviour alongside intellectual merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academy_selection_criteria_and_institutional_needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Good selections are not only for brilliance: the academy needs agreeable, light, sociable, worldly, witty companions; mediocrity 'shines' there. Randomness and occasional poor choices are necessary to preserve the institution's vitality and prevent it becoming inhospitable; mixing great and small personalities benefits both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for selection policies that balance excellence with sociability and institutional sustainability. When judging or designing learned societies, factor in social chemistry, entertainments, and the functional need for a range of temperaments rather than exclusive meritocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role_of_error_and_fortune_in_institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing chance and some errors in promotions or selections is essential; an institution that appeared infallible would become hateful. Occasional mistakes placate the public and save ego; the academy may even err purposely to preserve relations and avoid offending candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A guideline for institutional policy and optics: deliberate tolerance of imperfection can stabilize institutions, so assess decisions not only for 'correctness' but for their social and political effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: On_victory_as_the_measure_of_legitimacy_in_politics
rubrics_metrics.description: In political struggles, success is the sole judge of right and wrong—those who are defeated become 'rebels' regardless of moral claims. Parties are rarely cleanly divided into pure and impure; thus success determines legitimacy in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers a realist metric for evaluating political movements and legitimacy: be aware that legal/moral labels may be trumped by empirical success; useful for historical-political analysis of rebellions and regimes.
